newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Deputies unhappy about new Russia 97 budget plans.
newsitem.headline: Deputies unhappy about new Russia 97 budget plans.

text.p: Government ministers will meet leading parliamentians on Wednesday to try to break a deadlock over Russia's 1997 spending plans, but deputies said on Monday they were unhappy with the latest budget draft.

"It's an illusion, cosmetic changes," Alexander Pochinok, chairman of the tax sub-committee of the lower house of parliament, said of the government's new proposals. "They are just trying to tell deputies to take what they are given."
The government revised its 1997 spending plans last week after parliament rejected the first draft by a wide margin.

But the new budget figures differ only slightly from the old, shaving just under a trillion roubles ($180 million) from both income and expenditure and leaving the planned deficit unchanged at 3.3 percent of gross domestic product.

"I see already that the government has made the most superficial changes," Itar-Tass news agency quoted parliament chairman Gennady Seleznyov as saying. Seleznyov's Communist Party is the largest single faction in the lower house.
"The most acute social issues have not been adequately reflected in the government's new proposals."

Seleznyov will be one member of a conciliation commission of deputies and ministers which was set up after parliament rejected the government's first draft. The commission held its first preparatory meeting on Monday.

Deputies, aware of Russia's problems in meeting its 1996 tax collection plans, had complained when they voted the budget down that government revenue plans were not realistic and that the budget paid too little attention to the poor.

The new draft envisages raising 20 trillion roubles of 1997 tax revenue on Treasury bill operations, which are not taxed at present. The State Duma has already rejected a government proposal to impose a 15 percent tax on T-bills.
Other tax proposals include raising the income tax take on households to 7.54 trillion roubles in 1997 from a planned 5.88 trillion this year.

Proceeds from value-added tax are expected to rise to 149.8 trillion roubles in 1997, from a planned 113.3 trillion this year, although the government now expects only 79.7 trillion roubles in VAT this year.
This year's low tax collection has prompted the International Monetary Fund to delay a decision on whether to pay out the latest tranche of Russia's $10 billion IMF loan.
An IMF team of experts will return to Russia next month to reassess the figures.
